items.title: Big Cats, Small Prices – The Used Jaguars Worth Buying in 2026
items.summary: There's something undeniably special about owning a Jaguar. Whether it's the elegant styling, luxurious interiors or the unmistakable soundtrack of a supercharged V8, the British marque has spent decades building cars with character. But today, some of those same cars are available for remarkably little money. Years of depreciation have brought everything…
items.content_html:
We begin with one of Jaguar's most appealing modern bargains, the XE. Introduced in 2015 to challenge the BMW 3 Series and Mercedes-Benz C-Class, it combined sharp handling, handsome styling and a beautifully balanced rear-wheel-drive chassis.

Our research uncovered early 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol examples producing 240hp for under £6,000. These earlier Ford-derived petrol engines are particularly interesting alternatives to the more common Ingenium diesels, some of which have developed costly timing-chain problems.

The XE isn't perfect. Rear legroom is relatively tight, infotainment can feel dated and servicing costs remain those of a premium car. Nevertheless, for the money, few saloons offer quite the same combination of driving enjoyment and understated British character.

But before the XE, Jaguar had another compact executive saloon, and it's now even cheaper.


The X-Type arrived in 2001, bringing Jaguar ownership to a much broader audience. Although its Ford Mondeo connections attracted criticism, the X-Type offered attractive styling, comfortable interiors and a genuinely distinctive alternative to its German competitors.

Today, usable saloons can be found around £1,000, while our attention was drawn to the estate, with tidy examples available for under £2,000. Introduced in 2004, it combined Jaguar's traditional character with everyday practicality, making it particularly appealing as an inexpensive family car.

Petrol V6 models offer smooth performance, while diesels can be economical on longer journeys. However, rust around the sills, tired suspension and neglected maintenance deserve careful attention.


The XF Sportbrake takes the estate formula considerably further. Arriving in 2012, it combined the handsome styling of Jaguar's XF saloon with a spacious luggage compartment, comfortable seating and the sort of motorway refinement expected from a premium executive car.

Remarkably, our research uncovered examples from under £4,000, particularly those equipped with the 2.2-litre diesel engine. These offer a sensible balance of performance and economy, especially for drivers covering substantial annual mileages.

Higher specifications bring leather upholstery, attractive alloy wheels and generous equipment, making the XF feel considerably more expensive than its current asking price.

Buyers should check servicing, cambelt history, diesel particulate filter condition and electrical equipment. The larger V6 diesels offer stronger performance but can bring greater repair risks.

However, even the XF isn't Jaguar's grandest offering. For that, we turn to the flagship XJ.


For decades, the XJ represented the very best of Jaguar, combining effortless performance, elegant interiors and limousine-like comfort. Today, depreciation has made several generations surprisingly accessible.

XJs can be found for under £4,000, while examples with V8 power have appeared around £8,000. Our research even uncovered later XJR performance models around £20,000, offering extraordinary power and luxury for the money.

The aluminium-bodied X351 generation, introduced in 2009, marked a major departure from traditional Jaguar styling. Its sweeping dashboard, digital instruments and dramatic exterior brought the flagship firmly into the modern era.

Naturally, air suspension, complex electronics and powerful engines can generate substantial repair bills, so maintenance history is essential.


Few modern Jaguars have such distinctive styling as the S-Type. Launched in 1999, its rounded headlights, prominent grille and sweeping bodywork deliberately recalled the original S-Type of the 1960s.

Although controversial when new, that retro appearance has become part of its appeal. Our research found V6 petrol examples for under £2,000, with some V8 models available around £3,000.

Inside, traditional wood veneers, leather upholstery and a comfortable driving position create an atmosphere quite different from most modern executive saloons. The 3.0-litre petrol V6 is particularly appealing, delivering smooth performance without the running costs of the larger V8.

Age-related electrical faults, cooling-system problems and automatic gearbox condition deserve attention, while the 2.7-litre diesel carries additional mechanical risks.

The S-Type represents Jaguar looking proudly backwards. Our next choice is almost the complete opposite: a car that helped push the brand into an entirely electric future.


When Jaguar introduced the I-Pace in 2018, it became one of the first established premium manufacturers to offer a dedicated, fully electric performance SUV. Its futuristic styling, advanced electric architecture and remarkable acceleration made it a genuinely pioneering British luxury car.

Originally costing around £60,000, used examples can now be found from approximately £10,000. We identified one particularly interesting example at £10,350 with battery-health information available.

Twin electric motors provide all-wheel drive and 400PS, delivering performance that remains impressive today. The spacious interior, distinctive proportions and quiet driving experience also make it an appealing alternative to conventional premium SUVs.

However, battery condition is crucial. Certain I-Pace models have been affected by serious battery safety recalls, making confirmation of completed remedies and any charging restrictions essential before purchase.

For buyers wanting Jaguar SUV practicality without relying entirely on charging infrastructure, there's another option.


The F-Pace marked Jaguar's arrival in the premium SUV market in 2016, bringing sporting handling, generous interior space and distinctive styling.

Closely related in engineering to the Range Rover Velar, the F-Pace offers much of the appeal of a larger luxury SUV while retaining Jaguar's more driver-focused character.

Our research concentrated on the 3.0-litre supercharged petrol V6, uncovering examples from £12,490. With up to 380PS in higher-output versions, these offer genuinely impressive performance.

Fuel consumption can be substantial, but the V6 avoids the particular timing-chain concerns associated with some four-cylinder Ingenium diesels. Buyers should still inspect the cooling system, transmission, suspension and service records carefully.


Jaguar's smaller E-Pace arrived in 2017, offering much of the F-Pace's styling in a more manageable package. With a comfortable cabin, attractive proportions and practical five-door layout, it makes an appealing alternative to premium compact SUVs.

Our research uncovered 2.0-litre P250 petrol versions for under £9,000, bringing 250PS performance and all-wheel-drive capability at a particularly attractive price.

However, we were especially interested in the newer P300e plug-in hybrid, with examples appearing around £15,500. Combining a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with electric rear-wheel drive, it develops 309PS and originally offered up to 34 miles of electric range.

Regular home charging could make shorter journeys particularly inexpensive, although longer petrol-powered trips will be less economical than the headline hybrid figures suggest.

For buyers who don't need SUV practicality, Jaguar's traditional sporting coupés offer an entirely different experience.


Few cars capture Jaguar's sporting character quite like the F-Type. Introduced in 2013, it combined dramatic styling, a wonderfully purposeful driving position and a range of powerful engines, creating a genuine modern successor to Jaguar's celebrated sports cars.

Our research found early F-Types from approximately £17,000, while the formidable supercharged V8 F-Type R appeared around £24,000. That's remarkable value considering the performance and presence these cars deliver.

The supercharged V6 offers a particularly appealing balance of speed, sound and relative affordability, while the V8 provides an unmistakable soundtrack and extraordinary acceleration.

Running costs shouldn't be underestimated. Tyres, brakes, cooling-system components and specialist servicing can all be expensive, making a thorough inspection particularly worthwhile.

The F-Type delivers muscle, precision and modern sporting drama. However, buyers seeking a more relaxed grand tourer, with a traditional V8 as standard, should look towards its predecessor.


We finish with one of the most tempting Jaguar bargains of all, the second-generation XK. Introduced in 2006, this elegant grand tourer combined an aluminium body, beautifully proportioned styling and a naturally aspirated 4.2-litre V8 producing approximately 300bhp.

Our research uncovered early examples from around £6,000, while later 5.0-litre V8 models appeared closer to £9,000.

Unlike the more focused F-Type, the XK prioritises long-distance comfort, with supportive leather seats, generous front-seat space and a surprisingly practical hatchback-style boot. Certain specifications also offered traditional wood veneers, including burr walnut, a popular luxury-car finish when the model launched.

The rear seats are small, and fuel consumption certainly isn't modest. Buyers should also inspect the cooling system, suspension and electrical equipment.

Nevertheless, the XK delivers an extraordinary combination of V8 performance, comfort and understated elegance for remarkably little money.


From £1,000 X-Types to V8-powered grand tourers and sophisticated electric SUVs, the used Jaguar market offers an extraordinary variety of cars at prices that would once have seemed almost impossible.

Depreciation has undoubtedly created opportunities for buyers, but choosing carefully is essential. Engine selection, maintenance history and the availability of specialist support can make the difference between an enjoyable ownership experience and an expensive mistake.

Our advice is to prioritise condition over specification, budget realistically for maintenance and consider an independent Jaguar specialist inspection before committing to a purchase.

What makes these ten cars particularly interesting is how differently they interpret the Jaguar name. Some offer traditional luxury, others impressive practicality, while the F-Type and XK deliver genuine sports-car character.

For buyers prepared to do their research, a used Jaguar can still offer something special, often for considerably less than its badge and original price might suggest.

All vehicle prices reflect advertised UK used-market examples identified at the time of publication (14 November 2026). Prices, availability, mileage and vehicle condition may vary. Running costs and reliability considerations are provided as general guidance, and buyers should carry out independent checks before purchasing.

items.title: Reimagining Chrysler: Building the Next Generation of an American Icon
items.summary: For over a century, Chrysler has been one of America's most recognisable automotive brands. Founded in 1925, the company built its reputation on engineering innovation, affordable luxury and distinctive American design. From the groundbreaking Airflow of the 1930s to the imposing 300 saloons and generations of family vehicles, Chrysler has helped shape…
items.content_html:
Chrysler is still investing in its existing range. The 2027 Pacifica facelift introduces a striking new front end, illuminated wing badge, vertical LED lighting and updated interior details, demonstrating the brand's commitment to its current customers.

However, Stellantis' expansion plans point in a different direction. Rather than reviving the PT Cruiser or 300C, or developing a smaller Voyager, the focus is on a new family of SUVs. Historic nameplates, including Arrow and Airflow, offer a connection to Chrysler's past, while shared Stellantis platforms could make an expanded, more affordable range commercially viable.

The challenge now is creating vehicles that feel unmistakably Chrysler.


When Chrysler unveiled its Airflow concept in 2022, it offered a sleek, all-electric preview of the brand's future, alongside ambitious plans for an EV-only range. However, those plans have since changed.

After the original electric SUV programme was paused, a very different Airflow appeared briefly in a Stellantis presentation in June 2026. The newer design is more upright and practical, with sharper bodywork, distinctive vertical lighting and a full-width LED signature, all reflected in our TNY Design Studio rendering.

Expected for the 2028 model year, the new Airflow is expected to use Stellantis' flexible STLA One platform, supporting petrol, hybrid and fully electric powertrains. Early reports suggest petrol and hybrid versions could arrive first, replacing the original electric-only approach.

With pricing expected to start below $40,000, the Airflow could become an important foundation for Chrysler's expanding range.


Below the Airflow, Chrysler is planning two more affordable crossovers: the Arrow and Arrow Cross. Expected to start below $30,000, they could introduce the brand to a much broader audience, with both models anticipated around 2028.

Their foundations are already familiar in Europe. Based on the Fiat Grizzly family, both will use Stellantis' cost-effective Smart Car platform, shared with models including the Citroën C3 Aircross and Vauxhall Frontera.

The Arrow will adopt a sleeker coupé-SUV silhouette, while the Arrow Cross offers a more conventional, upright design. Petrol and mild-hybrid powertrains are expected to lead the American range, although final specifications remain unconfirmed.

Our Design Studio renderings explore how Chrysler's latest styling language could transform these affordable European foundations into something distinctly American, without the expense of developing entirely new vehicles.


The sleeker Chrysler Arrow could share its foundations with Fiat's new Grizzly Fastback, offering American buyers a more stylish alternative to the conventional SUV.

European models use Stellantis' familiar 1.2-litre turbocharged three-cylinder engine, available in petrol and mild-hybrid forms. However, American customers could be offered something different.

Stellantis has introduced a new-generation 1.6-litre turbocharged four-cylinder, manufactured in Michigan and powering the Jeep Cherokee's 210hp hybrid system. Could this engine, potentially in conventional petrol or hybrid form, find its way into Chrysler's smaller models?

Nothing has been confirmed, and adapting the engine to the Smart Car platform would require additional engineering. However, an American-built four-cylinder could offer stronger performance and greater appeal in the US market, while helping Chrysler establish a broader range of affordable vehicles.


Chrysler's future may ultimately depend on how successfully Stellantis can combine its global resources with the character and identity that made the American brand so recognisable.

The opportunity is certainly there. By sharing platforms, powertrains and components with established European models, Chrysler could introduce a broader, more competitive range without the enormous investment traditionally required to develop several new vehicles.

But affordability alone won't be enough. American buyers will expect distinctive styling, practical interiors, competitive performance and a convincing reason to choose Chrysler over increasingly capable rivals.

The Airflow, Arrow and Arrow Coupé imagined here at The New Yardstick Design Studio demonstrate how different segments could be brought together under a recognisable design language, while retaining their own personalities.

After years of contraction, Chrysler has an opportunity to become a more significant player in the American market once again. The next few years could determine whether that ambition becomes reality.

These renderings are independent artistic interpretations and are not official Chrysler or Stellantis designs. The New Yardstick is not affiliated with or endorsed by either company. Future vehicle specifications, pricing and launch dates remain subject to change.

items.title: 20 Years of Nissan Qashqai: How the Crossover Changed Britain, And What Comes Next
items.summary: Twenty years ago, Nissan took a gamble that would help reshape Britain's car market. Rather than develop another conventional family hatchback, the Japanese manufacturer introduced something different: a practical, affordable crossover combining the everyday usability of a hatchback with the raised driving position and styling of an SUV. The Nissan Qashqai arrived…
items.content_html:
When Nissan began developing a replacement for the Almera, it faced a difficult decision. Rather than compete directly with established hatchbacks such as the Ford Focus, Nissan took an entirely different direction.

The resulting Qashqai combined hatchback practicality with chunky, pseudo-off-roader styling, offering buyers the appearance and elevated seating position of an SUV without the running costs or bulk of a traditional 4x4.

Some early critics questioned the concept, but British buyers quickly embraced it. Sales exceeded Nissan's initial expectations, establishing the Qashqai as one of the manufacturer's biggest European successes. That success has endured, with more than 7.3 million Qashqai-family vehicles sold worldwide, including 4.1 million across Europe.

In 2008, Nissan expanded the range with the Qashqai+2, a stretched version offering seven seats, demonstrating just how versatile the crossover formula could become.

What initially looked like an unusual alternative to the family hatchback was rapidly becoming a blueprint for the industry.


By the time the second-generation Qashqai arrived in 2014, Nissan was enjoying a remarkable period of innovation. The GT-R had reinforced its performance credentials, the unconventional Juke had created another crossover success, and the Leaf had become the world's first mass-market, purpose-designed electric family car.

But the Qashqai remained central to Nissan's European business.

The second generation was longer, lower and more sophisticated, with sharper styling, improved interior quality and greater emphasis on technology and efficiency. The seven-seat Qashqai+2 disappeared, with Nissan directing larger families towards the X-Trail.

Crucially, the market had begun catching up. Rival manufacturers recognised the enormous potential of family crossovers, making the segment increasingly competitive.

Nissan could no longer rely on being different. It needed to demonstrate that the car which helped popularise the category could remain one of its strongest contenders.


By the arrival of the third-generation Qashqai in 2021, the crossover had become one of the most important vehicle types in Europe. Almost every major manufacturer was competing for buyers, while some brands had begun replacing traditional hatchbacks and saloons with SUVs and crossovers altogether.

Nissan responded with a more mature Qashqai, introducing fresh technology, a more spacious cabin and, subsequently, its distinctive e-POWER hybrid system.

Diesel engines disappeared from the range, leaving petrol mild-hybrid and e-POWER powertrains to meet changing customer expectations.

Competition, however, has never been fiercer. Established European, Japanese and Korean manufacturers are now joined by ambitious Chinese brands offering increasingly sophisticated and competitively priced alternatives.

The Qashqai's combination of practicality, comfort and familiar styling remains compelling, but its successor will enter a market considerably more demanding than the one Nissan helped create.


Looking at the lifespan of previous generations, a replacement for today's Qashqai might reasonably be expected around 2028 or 2029. However, recent reports suggest Nissan could instead introduce a substantial update, retaining much of the existing model's engineering.

The future of an electric Qashqai is also uncertain. Reuters reported in June 2026 that development had been halted, although Nissan has not formally ruled out an electric version. 

With the Leaf, forthcoming electric Juke and larger Ariya covering important parts of Nissan's EV range, the Qashqai could continue concentrating on petrol and hybrid technology.

Our Design Studio interpretation imagines a more modern, confident front end, incorporating Nissan's latest lighting signatures while retaining the familiar Qashqai proportions.

It's an evolutionary approach to a car whose established identity remains one of its greatest strengths.


From the rear, our proposed Qashqai continues that evolutionary approach. The familiar proportions remain, but cleaner surfaces, contemporary lighting and sharper detailing bring the design closer to Nissan's newest models.

Maintaining the Qashqai's position within Nissan's range will be particularly important. With the manufacturer investing heavily in electric vehicles, its petrol and hybrid models must remain equally competitive, offering customers a convincing alternative to going fully electric.

The next Qashqai doesn't necessarily need to reinvent the crossover. It needs to deliver the practicality, efficiency, comfort and value that made the original so successful, while introducing enough innovation to stand apart from an increasingly crowded field.

Twenty years ago, Nissan challenged the conventional family hatchback and helped change the direction of the British car market. Today, the crossover is everywhere, and the Qashqai faces more competition than ever before.

Its greatest challenge may no longer be convincing buyers to choose a crossover, but convincing them that the Qashqai is still the one to have.

Disclaimer: The fourth-generation Nissan Qashqai renderings are independent, unofficial design studies created by The New Yardstick. They are not affiliated with, endorsed by or commissioned by Nissan. Future model designs, specifications and launch dates remain speculative.

items.title: Electric Vans for Less – Britain's New and Nearly-New Bargains
items.summary: Electric vans have traditionally carried a substantial price premium over their diesel equivalents, making the switch difficult to justify for many British businesses. But the market is changing, and some of today's discounts are surprisingly substantial. From compact car-derived vans to full-sized commercial vehicles, both brand-new and barely used electric models are…
items.content_html:
TNY MARKET WATCH
Citroën ë-C3 Van 44kWh Plus
Manufacturer RRP £17,550 + VAT
Brand-new price £13,250 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £4,300 (24.5%)

At just £13,250 plus VAT for a brand-new example, the Citroën ë-C3 Van makes a compelling case for businesses that rarely need a full-sized commercial vehicle.

Based on the passenger ë-C3, it replaces the rear seats with a compact load area, retaining two front seats, familiar car-like driving manners and Citroën's comfort-focused suspension.

Its 44kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery offers approximately 200 miles of official WLTP range. LFP chemistry is particularly tolerant of regular charging to 100%, making more of that capacity available for everyday journeys without routinely limiting charging to 80%.

Another useful advantage is its towing capability. With a suitable approved towbar, the ë-C3 Van is rated to pull up to 550kg, potentially extending its appeal to businesses needing a small trailer. Its modest 300kg payload remains a limitation, but at this price, the little Citroën offers an appealing combination of affordability, versatility and low running costs.

TNY MARKET WATCH
DFSK EC35 39kWh 50 Auto SWB
Original manufacturer RRP £25,444 + VAT
Nearly-new price £6,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £18,449 (72.5%)

Few vehicles in this comparison illustrate the unusual electric van market quite like the DFSK EC35. We found several 2024-registered examples advertised at just £6,995 plus VAT, some showing only 99 miles. Their registration dates and remarkably low mileages suggest vehicles that have seen little commercial use, although their histories should be checked individually.

Despite its modest price, the Chinese-built EC35 offers a genuinely useful 4.8m³ load area, twin sliding side doors and a claimed payload of 1,015kg. Its 38.7kWh battery provides a quoted WLTP range of up to 166 miles in the 50mph-limited version.

That speed restriction is the major compromise: this is a van for local deliveries, estates and short, predictable routes rather than regular motorway work.

Buyers should also establish battery health, warranty coverage and servicing support before purchasing. Nevertheless, the combination of commercial carrying capacity and near-delivery mileage at this price is difficult to ignore.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Ford E-Transit Courier Trend 46kWh Auto
Manufacturer RRP £27,000 + VAT
Brand-new price £16,989 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £10,011 (37.1%)

The Ford E-Transit Courier is one of the smartest-looking small commercial vehicles on sale, combining SUV-inspired styling with the practicality businesses expect from a Transit. Its compact footprint makes it easy to manoeuvre and park, yet the squared-off load area offers approximately 2.9m³ of space for tools, parcels or local deliveries.

For 2026, Ford increased usable battery capacity from 43kWh to 46kWh, lifting the official range to around 201 miles, depending on specification. Rapid charging from 10–80% can take approximately 26 minutes using a suitable DC charger, making it more flexible for businesses working beyond a fixed local route.

With brand-new examples advertised from £16,989 plus VAT, the updated van is particularly difficult to overlook when lightly used 43kWh versions can cost around £16,000. At this price, buying new offers the longer range and the reassurance of a fresh vehicle warranty.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Ford Transit City 300S 56kWh Auto L1 H1
Manufacturer RRP £29,000 + VAT
Brand-new price £18,250 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £10,750 (37.1%)

Ford's new Transit City brings an interesting proposition to the electric van market, offering substantial carrying capacity at a price normally associated with smaller commercial vehicles.

Positioned between the E-Transit Courier and E-Transit Custom, the compact L1 model provides approximately 6m³ of load space and an impressive 1,085kg payload. Its three-seat cabin, practical sliding side door and relatively compact exterior dimensions make it particularly appealing for urban deliveries and tradespeople.

A 56kWh LFP battery provides up to 158 miles of official WLTP range, while DC charging from 10–80% takes approximately 33 minutes. Although its range is modest compared with some alternatives, the Transit City prioritises everyday working capability and affordability.

With brand-new examples advertised at £18,250 plus VAT, representing a substantial reduction against the £29,000 list price, this is a particularly attractive option for businesses. Our example is advertised for delivery in December 2026.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Kia PV5 Cargo Essential 51.5kWh Standard Range L2 H1
Manufacturer RRP £27,645 + VAT
Brand-new price £21,495 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £6,150 (22.2%)

The Kia PV5 is perhaps the most futuristic-looking van in this comparison, with its clean, upright front end, distinctive lighting and unusually spacious body. Unlike a converted passenger car, it was designed from the outset as an electric commercial vehicle.

Our brand-new Standard Range Essential offer costs £21,495 plus VAT. Its 51.5kWh battery provides up to approximately 184 miles of WLTP range, while the boxy load area offers 4.4m³ of space, accommodating two Euro pallets. A low loading step makes everyday deliveries easier.

For businesses covering longer distances, the 71.2kWh Long Range Essential is also available from just £23,995 plus VAT. Its official range reaches 258 miles, providing an additional 74 miles for £2,500 more.

With modern technology, a seven-year vehicle warranty and eight-year battery cover, the PV5 looks particularly competitive for a purpose-built electric van.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Mercedes-Benz eSprinter 314 81kWh PRO Auto RWD L3 H2
Manufacturer RRP £58,850 + VAT
Nearly-new price £26,895 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £31,955 (54.3%)

While significant discounts on smaller electric vans are becoming increasingly common, this Mercedes-Benz eSprinter stands out for its sheer size and capability.

The L3 H2 body offers an impressive 14m³ load area, paired with an 81kWh battery and rear-wheel drive. This is a full-sized commercial vehicle, suited to businesses transporting bulky goods rather than simply making short urban deliveries.

Our nearly-new 2025 example has covered just two miles, yet is advertised at £26,895 plus VAT, representing a saving of more than £31,000 against Mercedes-Benz's basic list price.

Even more remarkably, we've found a brand-new, unregistered example advertised at £27,855 plus VAT, just £960 more.

There are compromises, including an official range of approximately 161 miles and a relatively modest payload for such a large van. Nevertheless, these prices make the eSprinter a particularly compelling proposition for businesses considering electric transport.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Peugeot E-Expert 75kWh Professional Standard Auto
Manufacturer RRP £41,210 + VAT
Nearly-new price £15,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £25,215 (61.2%)

Few electric vans demonstrate the scale of today's discounts quite like the Peugeot E-Expert. A familiar choice among commercial fleets, the Expert is widely represented on Britain's used market, with numerous remarkably low-mileage electric examples currently advertised.

Our facelifted 2024 Professional example has covered just 143 miles and costs £15,995 plus VAT. Its 75kWh battery offers an official WLTP range of approximately 194–230 miles, depending on configuration, while the Standard body provides 5.3m³ of load space and a payload of around one tonne.

The facelift also introduces a redesigned front end, a more contemporary dashboard and a 10-inch infotainment touchscreen.

Buyers prepared to accept the older design have even cheaper choices. Pre-facelift 2024 examples with fewer than 200 miles start around £14,490 plus VAT, while we found another with 2,000 miles for £13,790. With such an abundance of nearly-new stock, the E-Expert is particularly difficult to overlook.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Renault Master E-Tech MM35 87kWh Advance Auto L2 H2
Manufacturer RRP £42,500 + VAT
Brand-new price £25,795 + VAT
BRAND-NEW SAVING £16,705 (39.3%)

The latest Renault Master is a particularly interesting entry, combining a genuinely modern large-van design with a substantial discount. Its distinctive front end and carefully developed aerodynamics help the 87kWh E-Tech achieve an official range of around 255 miles in this MM35 configuration.

The updated cabin is equally appealing, featuring a 10-inch touchscreen, practical storage and a more contemporary dashboard than many traditional commercial vehicles.

This L2 H2 version offers 10.8m³ of load space. Although larger versions provide considerably more room, the medium-length Master strikes a useful balance between carrying capacity and manoeuvrability. Its payload of approximately one tonne is worth considering for heavier loads.

With brand-new examples advertised at £25,795 plus VAT, the electric Master is now priced surprisingly close to some conventional diesel alternatives. For businesses needing a spacious van with respectable range and modern technology, it makes a compelling proposition.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Vauxhall Combo Electric 2300 Prime 50kWh Auto L1 H1
Original manufacturer RRP £33,300 + VAT
Nearly-new price £11,995 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £21,305 (64.0%)

The Vauxhall Combo is one of Britain's most familiar compact commercial vehicles, and its electric counterpart is becoming increasingly affordable. Our 2025-registered Prime example has covered just 3,353 miles, yet costs only £11,995 plus VAT.

This earlier 50kWh model offers up to 175 miles of official WLTP range. It misses out on the improved efficiency and potential 220-mile range of the newer 52kWh facelift, but remains well suited to predictable local journeys and overnight charging.

Despite its compact dimensions, the Combo Electric provides approximately 3.3m³ of load space and an indicative 803kg payload, making it useful for tradespeople and delivery businesses.

For those needing more room, we also found a long-wheelbase example with fewer than 100 miles advertised at £13,995 plus VAT.

With its established design, practical cabin and familiar driving experience, the Combo Electric offers considerable value for businesses willing to accept the shorter range.

TNY MARKET WATCH
Vauxhall Movano Electric 110kWh Prime Auto L3 H2
Original manufacturer RRP £50,385 + VAT
Nearly-new price £24,495 + VAT
NEARLY-NEW SAVING £25,890 (51.4%)

The Vauxhall Movano Electric rounds off our selection with one of the largest batteries available in this comparison. Our 2025-registered example has covered just 3,399 miles, yet is advertised at £24,495 plus VAT, less than half its original basic list price.

Its substantial 110kWh battery provides an official calculated combined range of approximately 235 miles in 3.5-tonne L3 H2 specification. The spacious 13m³ load area makes it suitable for bulky deliveries, removals and businesses requiring considerably more room than a compact van can offer.

The large battery limits payload to around 710kg in the 3.5-tonne version. However, the heavier 4.25-tonne Movano offers greater carrying capacity and can now be driven on a standard category B licence, thanks to recent changes in UK regulations.

With its modernised cabin, strong electric motor and significant discount, the Movano demonstrates just how accessible large electric commercial vehicles are becoming.

– The most striking finding isn't simply that electric vans are becoming cheaper, but how much choice buyers now have. From the £6,995 DFSK to heavily discounted large vans from Mercedes-Benz, Renault and Vauxhall, there are options for very different businesses and budgets.

Yet the lowest asking price isn't necessarily the best deal. Payload, driving range, charging access and the journeys a van makes every day remain important considerations. A local delivery business may find an ideal bargain here, while operators regularly covering longer distances or carrying heavy loads will need to choose more carefully.

What has changed is the starting point. With brand-new vans receiving substantial discounts and barely used examples appearing at a fraction of their original list prices, electric commercial vehicles deserve a fresh look from British businesses, including those that previously considered the switch too expensive.

Pricing and editorial notice: All prices exclude VAT and reflect advertised UK offers researched in November 2026. Savings compare advertised asking prices with manufacturer list prices, which may relate to different model years and include discounts or government grants. Prices, availability, specifications and eligibility may change. Figures are illustrative and should be confirmed with the selling dealer. WLTP ranges are manufacturer estimates; real-world performance varies.

items.title: Los Angeles Auto Show 2026: The New Cars, Concepts and Comebacks to Watch
items.summary: Los Angeles has always celebrated the automobile in its own distinctive way, and the 2026 LA Motor Show promises an intriguing mixture of traditional American muscle, cutting-edge electric technology and ambitious new designs. For American manufacturers, the direction of travel is becoming increasingly interesting. Powerful V8 engines are enjoying renewed attention, while…
items.content_html:
Ford heads to Los Angeles with one foot firmly in its performance heritage and the other in a very different future. The Mustang Dark Horse SC demonstrates that powerful combustion engines still have an audience, while the forthcoming Fathom could make electric pickups accessible to far more American buyers.

Confirmed for a 2027 launch, the Fathom is a five-seat midsize truck built on Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, with a planned starting price of $28,350. It will offer bidirectional power, allowing the vehicle to supply electricity to a suitably equipped home. Although Ford has revealed the name, technology and camouflaged prototypes, its finished design remains unseen.

TNY Design Studio has imagined how a production-ready Fathom might look, with a clean, purposeful front end and realistic pickup proportions. With Ford scheduled to address the media at LA, it is an especially relevant moment to consider what this affordable electric truck could become.


Ford's electric ambitions are only half the story in Los Angeles. The Mustang Dark Horse SC Convertible offers a striking counterpoint to the forthcoming Fathom, celebrating the power and theatre of traditional American muscle.

Powered by a supercharged 5.2-litre V8 producing 795 horsepower, it is the most powerful open-top Mustang Ford has ever built. A seven-speed dual-clutch transmission and specially tuned suspension combine formidable performance with the ability to enjoy longer journeys.

But there's more to this Mustang than its headline performance figures. California's open-top driving culture makes Los Angeles a natural stage for a Mustang that puts sound, performance and driver enjoyment at its centre.

With customer deliveries expected in spring 2027, the Dark Horse SC demonstrates that Ford's plans for affordable electric vehicles are developing alongside, rather than replacing, its enthusiast models.


Ford's plans extend far beyond the American vehicles appearing in Los Angeles. In Europe, the company is working with Renault Group on two affordable electric cars, the first expected in early 2028. Their shared underpinnings open up the possibility of a small Ford hatchback using the same platform family as the Renault 5 and Nissan Micra — and, potentially, the return of the Fiesta name.

Nothing has been confirmed about a Fiesta revival, and this is not a vehicle scheduled for LA. Nevertheless, the opportunity is certainly an interesting one. Ford withdrew the familiar Fiesta in 2023, leaving a gap in the supermini market just as affordable electric cars began gaining momentum.

TNY Design Studio's AmpR-based Fiesta rendering imagines how Ford might translate this new partnership into a recognisably Ford small hatchback, complementing the American-focused Fathom and Mustang stories.


Chevrolet is bringing one of America's most important pickups to Los Angeles: the completely redesigned 2027 Silverado 1500. Revealed earlier this year, the latest generation introduces more assertive styling, an extensively updated interior and considerably more technology.

Perhaps its biggest statement, however, lies beneath the bonnet. While much of the industry concentrates on electrification, Chevrolet has developed two entirely new V8 engines. The 5.7-litre produces 402 horsepower, while the larger 6.6-litre delivers 481 horsepower, reflecting the continued importance of conventional engines to American pickup buyers.

For Los Angeles, the Silverado provides an interesting contrast to the growing number of electric trucks. Rather than abandoning its established formula, Chevrolet is combining traditional V8 performance with modern driver assistance, digital technology and improved refinement.

It demonstrates that America's pickup market is evolving in several directions simultaneously, with familiar engineering remaining central to the industry's future.


With the sixth-generation Camaro gone, Chevrolet's performance-car range is now centred on the Corvette. But could Los Angeles offer the first clues about whether another, more accessible sports coupé might eventually join it?

Chevrolet has not announced a new Camaro, and there is no confirmed reveal scheduled for LA. Nevertheless, the show would be a fitting place to outline the next chapter for one of America's best-known muscle cars, particularly as Ford and Dodge continue developing high-performance models.

TNY Design Studio's hypothetical 2028 Camaro explores one possible direction. Our bright-yellow rendering combines familiar long-bonnet coupé proportions with a modern Chevrolet light signature, cleaner bodywork and a subtle ducktail spoiler, aiming for something that could plausibly reach production.

Whether its future involves V8 power, electrification or something between the two remains unknown, but the Camaro name is certainly one worth watching.


One of Cadillac's most exclusive recent performance models celebrates the brand's arrival in Formula 1 in 2026. The CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series is limited to just 26 cars and carries a revised 6.2-litre supercharged V8 producing 685 horsepower. It also retains a six-speed manual gearbox, an increasingly rare feature in high-performance luxury cars.

Behind those impressive figures lies a broader ambition. Cadillac is expanding its electric luxury range while using motorsport to strengthen its reputation against established performance brands. The combination reflects a manufacturer keen to explore new technologies without abandoning its sporting heritage. Cadillac is confirmed for Los Angeles, although this particular edition has not been announced as a show exhibit.

For TNY, it also provides a useful starting point for our speculative 2029 CT5 rendering, exploring how Cadillac's sporting saloon could evolve while retaining its distinctive American character.


Cadillac has made an increasingly unusual commitment: the CT5 will return for another generation. While much of the luxury market has shifted towards SUVs and crossovers, General Motors is still investing in a traditional sporting saloon, with a successor expected later this decade.

TNY Design Studio's hypothetical 2029 CT5 explores what that decision could produce. Finished in dark emerald green, our rendering develops Cadillac's signature vertical lighting with a slim horizontal lightbar and a cleaner, Celestiq-inspired grille, while retaining the long, low proportions that distinguish the CT5 from the brand's growing SUV family.

At Los Angeles, the electric three-row VISTIQ is confirmed for display. Cadillac could also use the occasion to discuss its plans for future V-Series models or offer further clues about the CT5 successor. For now, the production design remains under wraps.


Buick's appearance in Los Angeles will centre on the Enclave, the largest model in its American range. In flagship Avenir specification, the three-row SUV combines an elaborate grille, 22-inch wheels, a technology-rich cabin and available Super Cruise hands-free driving. It reflects how far Buick has moved from its traditional image as a maker of comfortable saloons.

The organisers have confirmed the Enclave for display, but no all-new Buick unveiling has yet been announced. Rather than a dramatic concept launch, LA looks set to give American buyers a closer look at the marque's increasingly premium SUV offering.

There is, however, another side to Buick. In China, the company is developing an extensive Electra range, including modern electrified saloons. That contrast raises an interesting question for the American market: could Buick eventually find room for a saloon again?


Buick's Electra L7 offers a glimpse of a side of the marque American buyers rarely see. Built for China, the sleek electrified saloon has a sweeping roofline and carefully detailed lighting that sit comfortably alongside Buick's newer design language. It also raises a question: could similar ideas eventually return to US showrooms?

TNY Design Studio's hypothetical 2028 Electra explores that possibility. Our burnt-orange saloon shares a family resemblance with the L7, but imagines a distinct North American interpretation, with its own front-end treatment and road-ready detailing. The connection is stylistic rather than a suggestion that the Chinese-market L7 itself is heading to America.

Reports have suggested GM is considering a new Buick saloon for the United States, although nothing has been officially announced. With Buick appearing at LA, even a small hint about its plans beyond SUVs would be worth watching.


Chrysler begins Stellantis’ Los Angeles story from an unusual position: its 2027 range revolves around a single nameplate, the Pacifica. The former Voyager has been absorbed into the Pacifica LX line-up, leaving the minivan to represent one of America’s oldest automotive marques.

For 2027, the Pacifica's higher trim levels receive a striking new face, with vertical LED headlights, an illuminated 'piano-key' grille, updated badging and additional driver-assistance features. It retains the clever Stow ’n Go seating and available all-wheel drive that have helped establish its reputation with American families. Already unveiled in New York, the facelift gets another opportunity to reach buyers in Los Angeles.

But Chrysler’s ambitions extend beyond people carriers. Stellantis has outlined plans for three additional Chrysler crossovers, including a mid-sized model and two smaller vehicles drawing on European platforms.

That expansion provides an intriguing starting point for TNY Design Studio’s own interpretation of the Chrysler Airflow.


Chrysler first unveiled its Airflow electric crossover concept at CES in 2022, introducing a sleek design, distinctive LED lighting and an emphasis on connected technology. Four years later, the brand is finally preparing to expand beyond the Pacifica.

Stellantis has confirmed a new mid-sized Chrysler crossover using its flexible STLA One platform, which can accommodate different powertrains. Although the production name remains unconfirmed, an Airflow-inspired SUV could offer the space, comfort and technology expected of a modern American family car.

Our 2028 TNY Design Studio rendering explores how that original concept might evolve into a realistic production model.

Two smaller crossovers are also planned, using European-derived platforms potentially related to the Fiat Grizzly and Grizzly Fastback. These could provide affordable entry points to Chrysler's expanding range.

Los Angeles might offer further clues about all three models, their designs and when American buyers can expect them.


Moving from Chrysler to fellow Stellantis brand Jeep, Los Angeles is less about an entirely new model and more about celebrating one of America's most recognisable off-roaders.

The 2027 Wrangler Switchback is the final instalment in Jeep's Twelve 4 Twelve programme, a year of special editions marking the brand's 85th anniversary.

Based on the Wrangler Rubicon X, the Switchback combines contrasting black and grey body panels with bright Gecko-green accents, distinctive graphics and matching wheel details. Available with two or four doors, it also receives exclusive Nappa leather upholstery and contrasting interior trim.

The real attraction at Los Angeles will be seeing all twelve special-edition Wranglers displayed together for the first time.

Although Jeep has no entirely new model confirmed for a debut at LA, the Switchback offers a reminder of the Wrangler's enduring appeal, its customisation possibilities and Jeep's considerable off-road heritage.


Stellantis’ move from Jeep to Ram brings one of Los Angeles’ most interesting themes into focus: the V8 is attracting renewed attention.

After years of manufacturers downsizing engines and investing heavily in electrification, the 2027 Ram 1500 Rumble Bee makes a decidedly old-school statement.

There are three HEMI V8 options: a 395hp 5.7-litre, a 470hp 6.4-litre and a supercharged 6.2-litre producing 777hp in the Rumble Bee SRT. Ram quotes 0–60mph in just 3.4 seconds for the flagship, placing it firmly in sports-car territory despite its pickup body.

The Rumble Bee revives the American muscle-truck formula, combining dramatic styling and serious performance with everyday practicality.

Alongside Ford's supercharged Mustang Dark Horse SC, it suggests that enthusiasm for large petrol engines remains strong. It may not reverse the industry's shift towards hybrids and electric vehicles, but it certainly makes this year's Los Angeles line-up more varied.


Following Ram's return to V8 power, attention naturally turns to Dodge and the possibility of another major comeback.

The latest Charger already offers electric Daytona and petrol SIXPACK powertrains, both available in two-door coupé and four-door saloon body styles. The twin-turbocharged 3.0-litre SIXPACK produces 420hp in R/T form or 550hp in Scat Pack specification, while the electric Daytona Scat Pack delivers an impressive 670hp.

However, one ingredient many traditional Dodge enthusiasts still want is a HEMI V8. Recent reports suggest a supercharged 6.2-litre V8 Charger could arrive for the 2028 model year, potentially restoring the unmistakable sound and character of the Hellcat.

Our TNY Design Studio rendering explores how such a model might look. Los Angeles could provide further clues, although Dodge has yet to confirm a V8 return. If it happens, the Charger could offer one of the most varied performance-car line-ups in America.


After the 777hp Ram and talk of a V8 Charger, Stellantis offers something completely different at Los Angeles: the Fiat Topolino. Measuring barely 2.5 metres long, this two-seat electric runabout sits at the opposite extreme of traditional American motoring.

Already introduced in the US, the 2027 Topolino gains new colours, an Open Air version and road-legal low-speed vehicle capability. With a maximum speed of 19mph, it isn't intended for freeways, but could suit neighbourhoods, resorts and short coastal journeys.

Priced at around $14,000, it also offers an unusually affordable entry point to electric mobility.

Its appearance at LA raises an interesting question: could Americans embrace something genuinely small alongside their enormous pickups and SUVs?

That concludes our look at America's major automotive groups. From Ford's electric ambitions and GM's luxury and performance models to Stellantis' V8 muscle and tiny electric runabouts, Los Angeles promises an extraordinarily varied collection of vehicles.


Moving beyond America's domestic manufacturers, Volkswagen brings a distinctly different perspective to Los Angeles with the redesigned 2027 Atlas Cross Sport. Developed around North American tastes, the five-seat SUV combines generous dimensions with a lower, more coupé-like profile than the seven-seat Atlas.

An updated 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine now produces 282hp, paired with an eight-speed automatic transmission and optional 4MOTION all-wheel drive.

Inside, Volkswagen has pushed the Cross Sport further upmarket, offering Nappa leather, genuine wood trim, massaging front seats and a 15-inch touchscreen with AI-powered voice assistance. The Atlas Cross Sport illustrates how Volkswagen adapts its products to American buyers, offering the space and equipment expected in this competitive SUV market.

Already unveiled earlier this year, its appearance at Los Angeles provides an opportunity for a closer look, while Volkswagen's scheduled media presentation could bring further details ahead of its showroom arrival.


Moving from Europe to Japan, Toyota brings one of Los Angeles' most important new family SUVs: the fully electric 2028 Highlander.

For a nameplate traditionally associated with petrol and hybrid power, the transformation is substantial. The fifth-generation Highlander becomes Toyota's first three-row electric SUV for the American market, offering seating for up to seven.

Buyers can choose front- or all-wheel drive, with 77kWh and 95.8kWh battery options. The larger battery delivers up to 315 miles of manufacturer-estimated range, while all-wheel-drive versions produce 338hp. A 14-inch touchscreen, spacious interior and vehicle-to-load technology add to its family appeal.

Crucially, the Highlander will also become Toyota's first electric vehicle assembled in America, with production planned for Kentucky and batteries sourced domestically. For a manufacturer that has long championed hybrids, this represents a considerable commitment to electric family transport. Los Angeles provides an opportunity for buyers to examine it ahead of its anticipated 2027 arrival.


Acura brings a different kind of Japanese innovation to Los Angeles with the NEXERA Vision, a dramatic coupé concept created at its own California design studio.

First unveiled at Monterey Car Week in August, NEXERA combines a low, muscular stance with butterfly doors, active aerodynamics and ultra-slim 'phantom' lighting that appears through the bodywork when illuminated. Its driver-focused cabin mixes forged carbon with sustainable materials, but the real purpose of the concept goes beyond creating an eye-catching showpiece.

Acura says NEXERA establishes the design language for its next generation of production cars, starting with the fourth-generation RDX Hybrid arriving in 2028. That SUV will also introduce Acura's two-motor hybrid technology, making the transformation more than cosmetic.

For Los Angeles, the NEXERA's appearance is particularly appropriate. Designed in the city itself, it offers visitors an opportunity to examine the styling details destined to influence Acura's future models.


From Japan, our Los Angeles preview moves to South Korea and the completely redesigned 2027 Hyundai Tucson, one of the most important family SUVs in Hyundai's American line-up.

Already unveiled in October, the new Tucson arrives with Hyundai's angular Art of Steel design language, giving it a more substantial, upright appearance. Increased dimensions promise additional passenger and luggage space, while the interior introduces Pleos Connect, Hyundai's next-generation infotainment system with AI-assisted voice control.

The hybrid is particularly interesting, with Hyundai targeting up to 42mpg on the American combined cycle, although final certified figures remain to be confirmed. Competing directly with the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V, the Tucson needs to deliver on practicality, technology and efficiency.

Los Angeles will give visitors a closer look at Hyundai's latest SUV, while the manufacturer has a separate global reveal scheduled for its 19 November press conference.


Staying with South Korea, Kia brings a very different proposition to Los Angeles: the 2027 Telluride Hybrid, a substantial three-row SUV designed with American families firmly in mind.

The second-generation Telluride actually made its debut at the 2025 LA Motor Show and is already on sale, making this year's appearance an opportunity to explore its first-ever hybrid powertrain.

Combining a turbocharged 2.5-litre petrol engine with electric assistance, it produces 329hp and 339lb ft of torque. Kia quotes up to 35mpg on the American combined cycle and an impressive potential driving range of 637 miles.

With bold, upright styling and a spacious interior, the Telluride demonstrates how hybrid technology can make larger family vehicles more economical without sacrificing performance.

Although not offered in Britain, it's an interesting example of how Kia is adapting its electrification strategy to American buyers.


To round off Hyundai Motor Group's Los Angeles presence, Genesis brings something considerably more extravagant: the GV90, its first full-size electric flagship SUV.

Unveiled in August 2026, the GV90 draws heavily from the striking Neolun concept, combining imposing proportions with an exceptionally luxurious interior. Available features include three-row seating, a retractable 24.6-inch OLED display and, on Neolun versions, dramatic coach-style doors with a concealed B-pillar.

Dual-motor versions offer up to 657hp, while American deliveries are expected to begin in early 2027.

The GV90 represents Genesis taking another ambitious step towards established luxury manufacturers, demonstrating that electric vehicles can offer considerably more than efficiency and performance.

From the family-focused Tucson and powerful Telluride Hybrid to the opulence of the GV90, Hyundai Motor Group's Los Angeles line-up illustrates just how far South Korean manufacturers have progressed — and how much further they intend to go.


We conclude our coverage of Asian manufacturers with one of Los Angeles' more unusual attractions: the FullGood Summer, a seven-seat plug-in hybrid from China with styling inspired by classic 1950s American vans. Its rounded bodywork, generous windows and distinctive proportions offer something refreshingly different from today's increasingly familiar SUV designs.

However, FullGood's appearance in Los Angeles is about considerably more than showcasing an interesting vehicle.

The Beijing-based manufacturer is making its American exhibition debut, with a dedicated press announcement on 19 November. It hopes to attract US investors, manufacturing partners and distributors, potentially allowing vehicles such as the Summer to be assembled and sold in America.

Nothing is guaranteed, but the company's ambitions are worth watching.

With no other Chinese passenger-car manufacturers currently confirmed for the show, FullGood provides an unexpected conclusion to our Asian coverage — combining nostalgic design, modern hybrid technology and genuine international ambition.

— If the 2026 Los Angeles Motor Show demonstrates anything, it is that the automotive industry no longer has one obvious direction. Powerful V8 engines are attracting renewed interest, electric vehicles are moving into increasingly varied segments, and hybrid technology is becoming central to everything from compact SUVs to large family vehicles.

American manufacturers are balancing familiar traditions with ambitious new products, while European and Asian brands continue adapting their offerings to one of the world's most influential car markets. There are also plenty of unanswered questions. Could Chevrolet revive the Camaro? How will Chrysler rebuild its range? And might new manufacturers such as FullGood eventually establish themselves in America?

Through our original TNY Design Studio renderings, we've explored some of those possibilities alongside the vehicles already confirmed.

With industry announcements scheduled for 19 November, Los Angeles could still deliver a few surprises. We'll be watching closely as speculation gives way to official news.

items.title: Small Cars, Smaller Prices? Exploring Britain's Used Microcar Market
items.summary: Small cars have been getting bigger for decades, but there's a corner of Britain's used-car market where compact dimensions remain the main attraction. From tiny diesel runabouts to characterful electric quadricycles, microcars offer an alternative for drivers who value easy parking, affordable motoring and simplicity over outright performance. But are they genuinely…
items.content_html:
The Aixam Coupé offers something increasingly unusual in our selection: compact urban motoring without a charging cable. Its two-cylinder Kubota diesel and CVT automatic will never win any races, but for short commutes, shopping trips and tight parking spaces, that simplicity has appeal.

Unlike the electric Ami, Twizy and Microlino, it can refuel at any diesel pump, making it particularly relevant to drivers without convenient home charging.

UK availability is limited. When we checked Auto Trader, just two 2013 diesel Coupés were advertised: a privately sold example with 21,800 miles at £4,350, and a lower-mileage dealer car with around 14,100 miles at £5,995. These are asking prices, not a reliable national average, and condition matters.

Fuel costs should remain modest for a low-mileage urban commuter, even with today's diesel prices. Insurance is another matter for younger drivers: our illustrative comprehensive quote for a 17-year-old came to £1,997.75. With a top speed of around 28mph, the Coupé remains very much a local runabout.

At just 2.41 metres long, the Citroën Ami is perhaps the purest expression of the modern urban microcar. Its two-seat cabin, tight turning circle and 28mph top speed make it particularly suited to short shopping trips, crowded streets and small parking spaces. Classified as a light quadricycle rather than a conventional car, motorway use is prohibited.

Used prices are becoming increasingly attractive, with examples advertised from around £4,600 when we checked. Its official range is up to 46 miles, while a full charge takes approximately four hours. For drivers covering relatively short distances with access to inexpensive home charging, electricity costs can be remarkably low.

Insurance is the catch for younger buyers. Our illustrative comprehensive quote for a 17-year-old came to £2,745.59, considerably more than the figure obtained for our experienced driver. Ultimately, the Ami makes most sense when its limited speed and range comfortably fit your everyday routine.

Certain versions of the Microcar M.Go offer something unusual among microcars: four seats. Its 505cc petrol engine and CVT automatic gearbox offer a practical alternative to the two-seat Aixam Coupé and Citroën Ami, particularly for short local journeys.

Crucially, this four-seat version is a heavy L7e quadricycle, rather than an L6e light quadricycle. It therefore cannot be driven at 16 on a category AM licence; drivers generally need a full category B car licence. Unlike 28mph L6e models, it can also reach higher speeds, although its lightweight construction deserves respect on faster roads. Like other quadricycles, it does not offer conventional-car levels of crash protection.

With examples advertised from around £2,500, it is among the cheapest vehicles to buy in our selection. Petrol costs should remain reasonable for urban commuters travelling just 3,000 miles annually. Insurance is another consideration: our illustrative comprehensive quotation for a 17-year-old came to £1,975.92.

The Microlino might be the most charming vehicle in our selection, but it is hardly the cheapest way into microcar ownership. Inspired by the classic BMW Isetta, its front-opening door, upright cabin and distinctive proportions make even an ordinary shopping trip feel like an occasion.

Unlike the Citroën Ami, the Microlino is an L7e heavy quadricycle capable of around 56mph, with seating for two and a surprisingly useful 230-litre boot.

We're looking at the 15kWh Long Range version, offering up to 142 miles between charges. Used 2025 examples have appeared from around £17,000, enough to buy a considerably more versatile conventional electric car. This makes the Microlino a purchase driven by affection as much as logic.

Electricity costs should be minimal for an urban commuter charging at home. Insurance is less forgiving for younger owners, however: our illustrative comprehensive quote for a 17-year-old came to £2,636.87. For enthusiasts who value personality over outright practicality, its appeal is obvious.

Few microcars have as much personality as the Renault Twizy. Its tandem seats, exposed sides and upward-opening doors make it feel more like an electric scooter with four wheels than a conventional car.

The UK-market Twizy 80 is an L7e heavy quadricycle, capable of 50mph and normally requiring a full car licence from 17. Renault claimed up to 62 miles per charge, although 37–50 miles is a more realistic everyday expectation.

Used prices now start around £4,000–£4,500, but battery ownership deserves particular attention. Many early Twizys were sold with a separate battery lease, historically costing around £50 a month — approximately £600 annually.

Some batteries have since been purchased outright, so buyers should check the current ownership arrangement even when an advert says "Battery Lease". Buyout prices vary, and a written settlement quotation should be obtained from Mobilize Financial Services rather than assuming a fixed purchase price. For young drivers, insurance could be the surprise attraction: our illustrative comprehensive quote for a 17-year-old was just £1,208.65.

The Fiat 500 provides an interesting comparison with our microcars. Despite its compact dimensions, it offers four seats, a useful boot and considerably more flexibility for longer journeys. Used 2016 examples with around 40,000 miles can be found for approximately £4,000, putting them directly alongside some of our featured microcars.

The familiar 69bhp 1.2-litre petrol engine has a manufacturer-claimed combined economy figure of 60.1mpg, while annual vehicle tax is just £20. At our assumed petrol price of 173.9p per litre, covering 3,000 miles would cost approximately £394.62 in fuel.

Our illustrative comprehensive insurance quote for a 30-year-old driver was £464.46, bringing estimated annual fuel, insurance and tax costs to £879.08, excluding maintenance.

For buyers who don't specifically need a microcar, the Fiat makes a compelling alternative. It remains small enough for urban use while offering considerably greater versatility, particularly for families and drivers regularly venturing beyond town.


The Smart Fortwo Electric Drive is a fascinating halfway point between a microcar and a conventional electric car. Measuring just 2.69 metres long, it is remarkably easy to park, yet offers proper car classification and a maximum speed of 80mph. Used 2017 examples can be found from around £7,000.

Its biggest limitation is range. Smart originally claimed 99 miles from the 17.6kWh battery, considerably less than the Microlino Long Range's 142-mile figure. Real-world range will generally be lower, particularly during winter.

Electricity costs are impressively modest. Using Smart's official consumption figure and our 9p overnight charging tariff, 3,000 miles would cost approximately £56.05.

However, annual tax is £200 for examples registered from April 2017, while our comprehensive insurance quote was £582.62. That produces an estimated annual total of £838.67. For urban drivers wanting something tiny without the compromises of quadricycle ownership, the Smart deserves consideration.

Purchase prices, servicing, MOTs, repairs, tyres, depreciation and other maintenance costs are excluded. Actual costs will vary.

Microcars are hardly a new invention. Long before the Citroën Ami, Renault Twizy and Microlino arrived, manufacturers were experimenting with tiny, economical vehicles designed to make everyday transport more accessible.

The BMW Isetta is perhaps the most recognisable example. We found a 1961 Isetta 300 advertised in Britain for £14,995, making it one of the most expensive vehicles in our selection, despite its age.

As a historic vehicle, it qualifies for free road tax, while specialist classic-car insurance could prove surprisingly affordable. However, fuel costs are less predictable, and maintaining a 65-year-old vehicle could require considerably more attention and expense. The Isetta is ultimately a charming classic to enjoy rather than a particularly sensible daily commuter.

So, are used microcars genuinely cheap to run?

Our comparison suggests that electric microcars have a clear advantage when it comes to everyday running costs. With inexpensive home charging and no vehicle tax, the Ami, Twizy and Microlino can offer remarkably affordable urban transport. The Twizy looks particularly attractive, provided its battery is owned outright.

Nevertheless, conventional small cars aren't necessarily far behind. The Fiat 500 and electric Smart Fortwo demonstrate that relatively inexpensive motoring doesn't require sacrificing quite so much practicality, speed or versatility.

But microcars aren't always purchased simply to save money. For some drivers, their tiny dimensions, effortless parking and suitability for short journeys are the real attractions. Others may specifically need a vehicle that can be driven on a category AM licence.

Ultimately, the best choice depends on how, where and why the vehicle will be used. For someone whose daily driving rarely ventures beyond their local town, a microcar could be all the transport they need.

Editorial notes and legal information

Prices, specifications, insurance quotations and running costs are illustrative UK figures researched in November 2026. Actual costs and availability will vary. Annual calculations assume 3,000 miles and the conditions stated alongside each vehicle. Purchase prices, servicing, repairs, MOTs and depreciation are excluded. Renault Twizy battery rental is also excluded.

The £230 vehicle-tax estimates for the Aixam Coupé and Microcar M.Go use DVLA's 2026–27 Private/Light Goods rates; individual classifications remain unverified. Other tax figures reflect the stated vehicle types and registration dates. Buyers should confirm tax, insurance and driving-licence requirements before purchasing.

items.title: Honda's Missing EV? Reimagining the Jazz for 2028
items.summary: For more than two decades, the Honda Jazz has earned a loyal following in Britain, combining compact dimensions with the space and practicality of a larger car. Yet as Honda develops a new generation of electric vehicles, its familiar supermini faces an intriguing question: could the next Jazz go fully electric? Britain's…
items.content_html:
Honda's next major electric arrival is the ALPHA, a compact SUV first previewed at the 2025 Japan Mobility Show. Built in India for global markets, its production version is scheduled to make its debut on 2 December 2026, with sales planned for 2027, initially focusing on India and Japan.

Official specifications remain under wraps, although a length of approximately 4.3–4.4 metres, front-wheel drive and battery options potentially ranging from 65–75kWh are anticipated.

For the Jazz, the ALPHA presents an intriguing possibility. If its electric architecture proves flexible enough, could Honda develop a shorter derivative for its established European supermini? Reducing the overall length to around 4.1 metres and introducing smaller 44–55kWh batteries could create an appealing alternative to the Renault 4.

With this in mind, TNY Design Studio has imagined how a fifth-generation Honda Jazz EV might look in 2028, combining familiar practicality with styling inspired by Honda's latest electric models.


Our imagined Jazz EV deliberately avoids the increasingly fashionable crossover look. At approximately 4.1 metres long, it retains the Jazz's upright silhouette, generous glass area and short bonnet, making the most of its compact footprint. A simple, modern front end introduces a little of Honda's Japanese kei-car character, without turning the Jazz into a miniature SUV.

That emphasis on practicality has always been part of the Jazz's appeal, and electrification needn't change it. We also see little reason to abandon the existing Jazz e:HEV immediately. An electric model could initially sit alongside today's efficient hybrid, giving customers two compact, genuinely practical Hondas to suit different lifestyles.

The challenge would be preserving the flexible seating, easy access and clever interior packaging that have made the Jazz such an enduring favourite. With so many small EVs chasing style, there's certainly room for one that puts space first.


Honda's new Super-N demonstrates just how much practicality can be squeezed into a tiny electric car. Measuring only 3.6 metres long, the Japanese kei-inspired hatchback accommodates four adults, features Honda's ingenious Magic Seats and offers remarkable versatility for its size.

Starting at £18,995, it isn't outrageously expensive either, particularly considering its generous equipment and distinctive character. Nevertheless, its 29.6kWh battery provides just 128 miles of WLTP combined range. That's perfectly reasonable for urban commuting or use as a second car, but considerably limits its appeal to drivers needing one vehicle for everything.

Competition is increasingly difficult to ignore, too. The Leapmotor T03 offers 165 miles of range for just £12,995. Meanwhile, larger electric alternatives offer considerably more space and range for around the same money.

This is precisely where an electric Jazz could make sense, combining Honda's clever approach to interior packaging with the space, battery capacity and range needed for everyday family motoring.


Honda's recent electric ventures haven't quite managed to replicate the success of its established hybrid models. The charming Honda e certainly looked the part, but its premium pricing and modest 137-mile WLTP range limited its appeal. The subsequent e:Ny1 SUV offered greater practicality, but with a launch price of £44,995 and a 256-mile range, it struggled to stand out against competitive European alternatives.

Honda closed UK orders for the e:Ny1 earlier in 2026, leaving the new Super-N as its only currently available electric passenger car in Britain.

That creates an increasingly difficult situation. The UK's zero-emission vehicle target rises from 38% in 2027 to 52% in 2028, before climbing to 66% in 2029. Meeting the 2028 target entirely through vehicle sales would require Honda to register more EVs than petrol and hybrid cars combined.

Manufacturers can purchase credits and use other regulatory flexibilities, but Honda faces an important decision: continue relying on such mechanisms or develop a broader electric range capable of attracting British and European buyers.

An electric Jazz, potentially joined by the ALPHA, could provide part of that answer.


The Civic has long been regarded as one of Honda's defining models, but British sales figures tell a surprisingly different story.

Since the Jazz arrived in 2002, approximately 460,000 examples have been registered in the UK through to the end of 2025. Over exactly the same period, the Civic managed around 483,000, just 5% more. In fact, the Jazz has outsold its more celebrated stablemate every year since 2009.

Across four generations, the Jazz has quietly become one of Honda's most important European nameplates, winning buyers through practicality, reliability and an ability to feel much bigger inside than its dimensions suggest. The Civic might attract more headlines, particularly in performance form, but the Jazz has played an equally important role in building Honda's loyal customer base.

Its future therefore deserves serious consideration, and an electric version could help ensure this remarkably successful little car remains relevant for another generation.



Editorial & Legal Notice: This article features an independent, speculative 2028 Honda Jazz EV concept created by The New Yardstick's TNY Design Studio. Honda has not confirmed an electric Jazz, its proposed specifications or any platform-sharing arrangement with the ALPHA. All predictions and renderings are for editorial and illustrative purposes only. The New Yardstick is not affiliated with or endorsed by Honda.
